offending.quoted_text: the court discussed the legislative purpose behind Section 437c(f)(2), highlighting that it was enacted to prevent abuse of the summary judgment procedure by disallowing multiple motions on the same issues.
offending.court_quote: Plaintiff asserts: “In Schimmel v. Levin (2011) 195 Cal.App.4th 81, the court discussed the legislative purpose behind Section 437c(f)(2) …” In fact, Schimmel does not contain a single reference to either summary judgment or section 437c.
offending.what_actually_exists: Schimmel v. Levin (2011) 195 Cal.App.4th 81 is a real California Court of Appeal decision that does not mention summary judgment or Code of Civil Procedure section 437c at all.

offending.quoted_text: Section 437c(f)(2) embodies a legislative judgment that a party should not be allowed to bring multiple motions for summary judgment based on the same issues without demonstrating newly discovered facts or circumstances or a change in the law. This policy applies even when the prior motion was denied on procedural grounds.
offending.court_quote: The quoted language does not appear in Schimmel—or in any other case of which we are aware.
offending.what_actually_exists: Schimmel is real; the quotation appears neither in it nor, so far as the court was aware, in any other case.

offending.as_cited: Regency Health Services, Inc. v. Superior Court (1998) 64 Cal.App.4th 1496, 1504
offending.cited_case_name: Regency Health Services, Inc. v. Superior Court
offending.quoted_text: A continuance should not be granted when it is sought to facilitate procedural maneuvers rather than to promote justice.
offending.court_quote: Regency does not address the granting of a continuance, and the quoted language does not appear anywhere in the opinion.
offending.what_actually_exists: Regency Health Services, Inc. v. Superior Court (1998) 64 Cal.App.4th 1496 is real but does not address the granting of a continuance and contains no such language.

offending.quoted_text: emphasized that filing a second dispositive motion without new facts or law is frivolous and subject to sanctions
offending.court_quote: Peake does not address the filing of a second dispositive motion, and the only sanctions at issue in that case were for filing a frivolous pleading. (Id. at pp. 432–450.)
offending.what_actually_exists: Peake v. Underwood (2014) 227 Cal.App.4th 428 is real; the only sanctions at issue there were for filing a frivolous pleading.

offending.as_cited: Goldstine v. Liberty Mut. Ins. Co., 2020 WL 6216738 (W.D. Wash. 2020)
offending.cited_case_name: Goldstine v. Liberty Mut. Ins. Co.
offending.quoted_text: where sanctions were imposed for similar baseless claims of personal hardship to delay proceedings
offending.court_quote: Goldstine appears to be a fabricated case.

The words “frivolous,” “unfair,” and “tactics” do not appear in Heckert, which concerns the appellants' claim that the trial court erred by refusing to order their real estate broker to pay their attorney fees as damages.
offending.what_actually_exists: Heckert v. MacDonald (1989) 208 Cal.App.3d 832 is real and concerns a claim that the trial court erred by refusing to order the appellants' real estate broker to pay their attorney fees as damages.

offending.as_cited: [Aggregate finding] 21 of the 23 case quotations in appellant's opening brief
offending.cited_case_name: multiple — not itemised beyond the examples above
offending.filing: Appellant's opening brief and reply brief
offending.court_quote: In total, appellant's opening brief contains 23 case quotations, 21 of which are fabrications. Appellant's reply brief contains many more fabricated quotations. And, both briefs are peppered with inaccurate citations that do not support the propositions for which they are cited.
offending.what_actually_exists: The court noted that “although most of the cases to which the quotes are attributed exist, the quotes do not,” and that a few of the cited cases do not exist at all.

controls.cited_for: that a fake opinion is not existing law and citing one provides no non-frivolous ground for extending, modifying or reversing existing law
controls.court_quote: “A fake opinion is not ‘existing law’ and citation to a fake opinion does not provide a non-frivolous ground for extending, modifying, or reversing existing law, or for establishing new law. An attempt to persuade a court or oppose an adversary by relying on fake opinions is an abuse of the adversary system.” (Mata v. Avianca, Inc. (S.D.N.Y. 2023) 678 F.Supp.3d 443, 461, fn. omitted.)

controls.as_cited: Kruse v. Karlen (Mo. Ct. App. 2024) 692 S.W.3d 43, 52
controls.cited_for: that filing an appellate brief with bogus citations cannot be countenanced and is a flagrant violation of the duty of candor
controls.court_quote: Kruse v. Karlen (Mo. Ct. App. 2024) 692 S.W.3d 43, 52 [“Filing an appellate brief with bogus citations in this Court for any reason cannot be countenanced and represents a flagrant violation of the duties of candor Appellant owes to this Court”]

controls.as_cited: Benjamin v. Costco Wholesale Corporation (E.D.N.Y. 2025) 779 F.Supp.3d 341, 343, 347
controls.cited_for: that an attorney who submits fake cases clearly has not read them, and that courts across the country have issued a panoply of sanctions
controls.court_quote: See Benjamin v. Costco Wholesale Corporation, supra, 779 F.Supp.3d at p. 343 [“an attorney who submits fake cases clearly has not read those nonexistent cases, which is a violation of [the federal equivalent of § 128.7]”]

controls.as_cited: Garner v. Kadince, Inc. (Utah Ct. App. 2025) 571 P.3d 812, 816
controls.cited_for: sanctioning counsel for filing appellate briefs containing fabricated legal authority
controls.court_quote: Garner v. Kadince, Inc. (Utah Ct. App. 2025) 571 P.3d 812, 816 [sanctioning counsel for filing appellate briefs containing fabricated legal authority]

controls.cited_for: that little is gained by dismissing an appeal rather than deciding it on the merits once the record has been reviewed thoroughly
controls.court_quote: (See People v. Wende (1979) 25 Cal.3d 436, 443 [affirming on the merits rather than dismissing appeal as frivolous: “Once the record has been reviewed thoroughly, little appears to be gained by dismissing the appeal rather than deciding it on its merits”].)

controls.cited_for: that a sanctions order is reviewed for abuse of discretion
controls.court_quote: We review a sanctions order for an abuse of discretion. (McCluskey v. Henry (2020) 56 Cal.App.5th 1197, 1205.)

controls.as_cited: Mansell v. Board of Administration (1994) 30 Cal.App.4th 539, 546
controls.cited_for: that it is not the court's function to serve as an appellant's backup appellate counsel
controls.court_quote: Moreover, “it is not this court's function to serve as [appellant's] backup appellate counsel.” (Mansell v. Board of Administration (1994) 30 Cal.App.4th 539, 546.)
